text: Chapter 1 Introduction In science and technology, we see random change and patterns of variation due to chance. Whether - changes in weather or climate; - spread of disease; - traffic congestion; - noise or shut-down in communication systems; - quality variation in a manufacturing line; - intrinsic randomness in the evolution of all living species, or something else. These course notes give an introduction to some of the mathematical ideas, tools, and models that are widely used to study the basic mechanisms of randomness in such systems. The notes provide a semi-rigorous mathematical introduction to a collection of models based on the theory of probability and stochastic processes, and cover a number of examples from computer science and communication engineering where these models come to use. The selection of material starts at the level of a standard course in introductory probability and statistics, but does not assume prior knowledge of stochastic processes. We begin with a brief review of tools from probability theory, including the notions of independence, expected value, variance and covariance, as well as those of the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem. Then we introduce basic concepts and ideas of stochastic processes for studying stochastic models and give introductory examples of random processes. This is followed by a discussion on how to instruct a computer to simulate random behavior. We discuss briefly the theoretical background of computer simulation of stochastic processes and look at some examples of simulation code. Additional

Chapter 2 Introduction Mathematical modeling in many areas of science and technology must take into account elements of chance and randomness. Methods from elementary probability theory and sta- tistics are sufficient in situations such as analyzing a sample of data subject to measurement errors, but further ideas from the theory of stochastic processes are essential to properly understand random dynamics and random evolution. The concept of a random variable as a value determined by the outcome of a random experiment is central in probability theory. Following standard practice in denoting random variables with capital letters X, Y , etc, we recall that the distribution function of a random variable X, defined by F (x) = P (X≤x ), completely specifies the nature of the random fluctuations in X that occur when performing the experiment. The expected value E(X) and the variance V (X) of X, when they exist, are the standard means of measuring “average value” and “average variation” of random variables. Consequently, the first steps in stochastic modeling are to identify relevant random variables and study their distributions and other characteristics, such as expected values and variances. We begin this chapter with a few definitions of concepts and ideas that are useful for studying stochastic models. Some introductory examples of random processes are given, where we recall from probability theory the notions of independence, expected value, variance, and covariance, as well as those of the law of large numbers and the central limit

theorem. This is followed by a short discussion on the topic of how to instruct a computer to simulate random behavior. Then we present two basic stochastic models in more detail. First, we have the life-length process, which describes events that occur after a random time. One may think of the failure time of a mechanical device or the life-length of a human being as examples. Secondly, the Poisson process is the fundamental model for a series of events that occur randomly at any point in time and independently of each other. The series of times of decay of a radioactive source is a standard example of a real-world phenomenon where the Poisson process provides the mathematical description and where the fit between the two is exceptional. 2.1. text: 2.1. Stochastic processes11 Any collection of independent random variables trivially forms a stochastic process. We encounter this example later in discrete time with the designationwhite noise. However, there is usually some statistical dependence, between the outcomes X(t1) and X(t2) of a random process {X(t)} sampled at two time points t1 and t2. In fact, most of the interesting stochastic processes that are used in theory and applications fall into one of several categories of processes, each characterized by a particular dependence structure over time. Such categories we will make acquaintance with are stochastic processes with independent increments, stationary processes, Markov processes, and renewal processes. For some examples of random processes, but not all, it is appropriate to measure the dependence along the paths by means of the covariance function C(X(t 1), X(t2)) =E(X(t 1)X(t 2))−E(X(t 1))E(X(t 2)). As the terminology of discrete and continuous time introduced above already suggests, stochastic processes often describe the evolution over time of randomly varying quantities. Galton’s Bean Machine The bean machine, also known as the Galton box orquincunx, is a device invented by Sir Francis Galton (1822-1911) to demonstrate the central limit theorem. A large number of balls, spherical “beans”, are dropped from the same position at the top of a vertical board with interleaved rows of metal pins and one-ball-wide bins at the bottom. Each ball bounces randomly left or right with equal probability once every row and ends up in one of the collecting bins. The number of balls in each bin viewed together forms an approximate Gauss curve. Why? Suppose there arenrows on the board, consider a single ball, and put Xn = number of jumps to the right minus number of jumps to the left. In other words, the ball lands in bin Xn if the bins are numbered with bin 0 at the center. Our mathematical model of the Galton box is now that each ball follows the path of a symmetric random walk as in 2.2 withp= 1/2. In particular, E(Zk) = 1·0.5 + (−1)·0.5 = 0, E(Z 2 k) = 12 ·0.5 + (−1) 2 ·0.5 = 1, V(Z k) = 1 so that E(Xn) = 0, V(X n) =n and hence, by the central limit theorem, Xn is approximately normal with distribution N(0, n). It is the shape of this distribution which begins to form at the bottom of the bean machine board after a sufficient number of balls have been dropped.

text: 202. Introduction Pseudo-random numbers.Standard methods for computer simulations are based on entirely different principles. The standard technique is to use a pseudo-random number generator. This is an algorithm in the form of a few lines of program code. The input to the program is an arbitrary number, aseed, such as given by the current clock time, and the output is the first pseudo-random number. When the procedure is repeated, each time executing the code with the most recent output as new input, the result is a sequence of pseudo-random numbers. Hence pseudo-random numbers are entirely deterministic and predictable, since the same seed will always produce the same sequence. Sooner or later the sequence must even begin repeating itself since the computer stores only a finite number of digits, and hence pseudo-random sequences are necessarily periodic. But what matters is that the underlying algorithm can be designed so that pseudo-random numbers “look like” and behave as if they were true random numbers. text: Example 3.33.The Galton-Watson branching model describes the evolution in a popula- tion where all individuals have equal lifelengths and they all reproduce independently of each other according to the same mechanism. More exactly, an individual which is born at time n− 1 dies at time n and replaces itself upon death with a random number of offspring. The number of newborn individuals is chosen according to a given probability distribution ν = {νk}k≥0, the offspring distribution. The new members of the population repeat the life pattern of their parents and act independently of any other individual. In particular, with probability ν0 an individual leaves no offspring in the next generation and hence in no future generation of the population. It turns out that the general behavior of the branching mechanism to a large extent is determined by the mean offspring parameter m =P k kνk. Branching processes with m < 1, m = 1 and m > 1 are called subcritical, critical and supercritical, respectively.
